newsitem.title: CHINA: HK lawmakers make Japan island protest in Beijing.
newsitem.headline: HK lawmakers make Japan island protest in Beijing.

text.p: Hong Kong legislators on Thursday protested against Tokyo's control of a group of disputed islands in the East China Sea by handing in letters to the Japanese and U.S. embassies in Beijing, reporters and diplomats said.
Chinese police outside the Japanese embassy confiscated video tapes from reporters covering the arrival of the lawmakers and told them to leave the area, journalists said.

In a letter to Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, Hong Kong Legislative Council member Frederick Fung called on Tokyo to renounce its claim to the islands, known in Chinese as the Diaoyus and in Japan as the Senkakus.
A long-standing dispute over the islands has flared in recent months after Japanese rightwingers moved to bolster Tokyo's claim by building a lighthouse on one island in the group.
The row has united nationalist sentiment in China, political arch-rival Taiwan and the British colony of Hong Kong, which reverts to Beijing rule on July 1, 1997.

Japan was to blame for the death of Hong Kong "martyr" David Chan in the waters near the uninhabited but potentially resource-rich islands, wrote Fung, who is also chairman of the Hong Kong Association for Democracy and People's Livelihood.
Activist Chan drowned last week after leaping from a Hong Kong ship into stormy seas near the islands to protest Tokyo's control over them.
A Japanese coast guard medical team was unable to revive Chan but saved the life of a co-protester who also jumped into the water after Japanese vessels blocked an attempt to land on the islands.

In a letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton handed in to the U.S. embassy, Fung wrote that Washington should apologise to China for returning the Diaoyus to Japan in the early 1970s and called for the United States to support Beijing's claim.
He did not explain why the letter was being delivered in the Chinese capital instead of via U.S. diplomats in Hong Kong.
A Hong Kong reporter who covered Fung's arrival at the Japanese embassy said Chinese police confiscated at least three videotapes from reporters and ordered them to leave the area.
"The police said that this was a very sensitive moment," said the reporter, who declined to be identified.
